messages.content:
Implement one complete standalone child-facing HTML evaluation from the immutable academic and design artifacts.

Implement the artifacts faithfully. You own implementation details needed to make the declared interaction work, but you may not add another design doctrine, change academic content, expose an answer before the first committed response, or make learning conclusions.

The document must work at the declared viewport with touch and mouse and no keyboard requirement. The child must always be able to continue after an incorrect, uncertain, or instrument-ambiguous response. Every queried DOM element must exist before JavaScript accesses it. Use no parent application endpoints, cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, currency, browser speech synthesis, or oscillator audio.

Post evaluation_ready, evaluation_attempt, evaluation_friction, and evaluation_complete messages to window.parent. Every attempt must include itemId, constructId, result, assistance, exposure, responseMode, possibleConfounds, and attemptedValue. Return one complete HTML document and nothing else.

TARGET VIEWPORT
1365×768

{
  "artifactId": "design:LAB-MATH-GEOMETRY-FACES-5-11:opening:museum-vault:v1",
  "upstreamHash": "357e7ae9a9243586a072d9bb454180bf3f7fb63793f6cec1128c39b2781cffb0",
  "title": "The Shape Museum: Vault of Five Doors",
  "designRationale": "The contract requires five fixed-order items measuring flat/curved discrimination, face-shape identification, the sphere special case, and face-set reasoning, with zero teaching, zero feedback, and zero answer exposure before completion. The core design problem is making a no-feedback experience feel purposeful to a nine-year-old who has evidenced appetite for hard problems and skepticism about faulty logic (reina:riddles:harder, reina:riddles:logic). The solution: a Shape Museum where the child is the newly hired Night Inspector who must file five inspection reports to open the sealed Vault. Filing a report is inherently commitment-based — museums accept reports without arguing back — which makes the absence of correctness feedback diegetic and honest rather than withheld. Each submitted report visibly stamps and slides into a slot beside one of five vault doors; the world reacts to the ACT of committing (stamp, door mechanism turning), never to correctness. Evidence of the child valuing difficulty and questioning logic informed tone (she is treated as a professional inspector, not a student) but was not used to invent a preference: no riddle mechanic, no hint content, no examples were added, because the contract's hintPolicy forbids them. The small-sample feedback favoring color and clear visuals is honored through high-contrast solid renders with the queried face highlighted in a single saturated accent color, exactly as the instrumentHypothesis directs. A visible non-teaching 'Ask the Curator' button satisfies the hintRequested measurement key: pressing it restates only the response format ('Tap one card, then press FILE REPORT'), never geometry content, and the press is logged. Skips are diegetic ('File as Unresolved') so declining never feels like failure and never traps the child. All exposure identities, orientations, option lists, and scoring rules are rendered verbatim from the contract; the design layer adds only framing, pacing, and dignity.",
  "independentlyChosenPrinciples": [
    "Commitment before revelation: every world reaction responds to the act of filing, never to correctness, so the no-feedback rule reads as world logic instead of withheld information.",
    "The construct is the only hard thing: all controls are large tap targets (min 96px), no typing, no dragging, no timing, no reading beyond contract prompt text, so response mode never becomes the measured skill.",
    "Dignity by role: the child is cast as a competent professional whose reports are trusted; skipping is a legitimate professional action ('Unresolved'), not a defeat state.",
    "Diegetic instrumentation: hint requests, skips, option changes, and latency are captured through in-world actions the child would take anyway, keeping measurement invisible and evidence uncontaminated.",
    "Honest payoff: the vault opens on completion (all five items terminal), not on score, so the reward never leaks correctness and never punishes wrong answers.",
    "One screen, one decision: each item is a single full-screen scene with prompt, contract-verbatim pictures, and option cards; nothing else competes for attention on the 1365×768 viewport.",
    "Fresh eyes per door: no solid image, highlight, or option from one item ever remains visible during another, protecting the contract's doesNotRevealAnswersTo guarantees."
  ],
  "openingPromise": "A short animated title card: \"The Shape Museum needs a Night Inspector. Five vault doors are sealed. Only your five inspection reports can open them. Nobody has seen what's inside.\" One large glowing button: \"START INSPECTION.\" The promise is concrete, immediate, and mysterious — file five reports, open the vault — and requires no reading beyond two sentences.",
  "firstThreeSeconds": "Second 0–1: dim museum hall fades in; five brass vault doors glint in a row; a lantern glow follows an inspector badge that slides to the child with her title on it. Second 1–2: the first door pulses softly and a pedestal rises in front of it carrying the I1 exhibit (cylinder, sphere, rectangular prism, cone, upright standard views, clearly lit and color-separated). Second 2–3: the prompt appears in large type with four big answer cards fanning out below it, and the pulsing outline settles on the cards — visually saying \"your move.\" No tutorial, no narration required; the first tap target is unmistakable.",
  "firstAction": "Tap one of four large labeled answer cards (\"the cylinder,\" \"the sphere,\" \"the rectangular prism,\" \"the cone\") beneath the I1 exhibit, then tap the large \"FILE REPORT\" stamp button that activates once a card is selected. Selecting a card highlights it; re-tapping another card changes the selection (each change logged as optionChangeCount). Nothing is committed until FILE REPORT is pressed.",
  "mission": "As the museum's Night Inspector, examine five exhibits of solid figures and file one inspection report per exhibit describing their surfaces and faces. When all five reports are filed (or marked Unresolved), the vault's five-lock mechanism releases and the sealed vault opens, revealing the museum's hidden centerpiece. The mission is completion of honest reports, not correctness — the child is told the museum \"trusts your judgment and files every report exactly as you write it.\"",
  "coreInteraction": "Each of the five doors presents one contract item as an exhibit scene: contract-verbatim prompt (under 25 words, large type, optionally read aloud via a tap-to-listen speaker icon so reading is never the barrier), the exact solids/orientation/highlight specified by the item's exposureIdentity, and the exact option list as large tap cards. Single-select items (I1, I2, I4): tap one card, FILE REPORT. Multi-select items (I3, I5): cards toggle on/off with visible checkmarks; the selectionRule is shown in plain words (\"Pick every true statement — there can be more than one\"); I5 enforces the contract rule that 'none of them' deselects all others and vice versa, with a gentle wobble animation explaining the exclusivity without teaching content. Every item screen also offers 'Ask the Curator' (logs hintRequested; returns only format restatement) and 'File as Unresolved' (logs noResponse skip). After FILE REPORT, the report card stamps, slides into the door's slot, one lock wheel turns, and the next exhibit rises. The interaction loop is: observe exhibit → decide → select → commit → advance. Independent response always precedes any support, and no support with geometric content exists anywhere in the experience.",
  "mathAsPower": "The child's geometric judgment is literally the key mechanism: each report is a claim about flat faces, curved surfaces, and face composition, and only a filed claim turns a lock wheel. Deciding whether a sphere has any flat face (C1/C3), naming the circle atop the cylinder (C2), asserting the cone's coexisting flat face and curved surface (C1), and composing the pyramid's full face set against its triangle silhouette (C4) are the only actions that move the world forward. No other verb exists in the experience — you cannot fight, collect, or dodge your way to the vault; you can only reason about surfaces and commit. The causal chain is: mathematical judgment → filed report → lock turns → world advances → vault opens.",
  "responseAffordances": "All responses are large tap cards (minimum 96×96px hit area, generous spacing) usable by touch or mouse with no precision demand, no drag, no typing, no keyboard, no scrolling within an item. Text is large (minimum 24px) with a tap-to-listen audio read-aloud on the prompt and on each option card so reading skill is not the construct. Selection is two-stage (select, then FILE REPORT) so accidental taps never commit; changing selection before filing is free and logged, never penalized. Multi-select cards show explicit checkmarks and a live count (\"2 statements picked\") so the child can see the format state. Color highlighting of the queried face (I2's top face) uses a saturated accent plus a hatched texture ring so color-vision differences don't gate the item. Nothing about the interface must be discovered: every actionable element pulses once when the screen loads, and the Curator button restates format on request.",
  "stakesAndConsequences": "Stakes are narrative and forward-moving: each filed report permanently turns one of five lock wheels, and the vault cannot open until all five doors have a filed or Unresolved report. Reports are final once stamped — the museum \"archives every report the moment it's stamped\" — which makes commitment meaningful and protects evidence integrity (no revisiting, no answer-shopping). Consequences never touch correctness: a wrong report turns its lock wheel exactly like a right one, an Unresolved report turns it with a grey seal instead of a wax seal, and the vault opens either way. What's at stake is the child's professional act of judgment and the mystery behind the vault, not a score, a grade, or an approval signal. Dignity is preserved because the world treats every committed judgment as valid inspector work.",
  "recovery": "No state traps the child. Uncertain: 'File as Unresolved' is always visible, phrased as legitimate inspector procedure, logged as noResponse (contract: not scored incorrect), and advances to the next door. Interface confusion: 'Ask the Curator' restates navigation/format only (contract-permitted non-teaching clarification) and is logged as hintRequested; the item is scored as-is per hintPolicy. Accidental tap: two-stage commit means a stray tap only changes selection, never files. Multi-select exclusivity (I5): choosing 'none of them' while others are selected triggers a wobble and auto-clears with a one-line format note, preventing an invalid-state trap. Wanting to stop: an always-available 'End Shift' door in the corner lets the child exit after any item; remaining items log as notAdministered, and the exit scene thanks the Inspector for the reports filed with no vault-denied shaming (the vault simply \"waits for the next shift\"). Nothing ever loops the child back to a failed state, demands a retry, or blocks progress on a wrong answer.",
  "progression": "A persistent but unobtrusive strip along the top shows the five vault doors; each terminal item stamps a seal on its door (wax seal for filed, grey seal for Unresolved) and turns its lock wheel with a satisfying mechanical rotation. Items run in the fixed contract order I1→I5, each as a fresh scene with prior exhibits fully removed. Between items a two-second transit beat (lantern glide down the hall) provides pacing without content. The fifth stamp triggers the five wheels spinning in sequence and the vault unlocking.
